title: A friend to myself
hook: Hecaton says: I have begun to be a friend to myself

segments.voice: Yesterday: hope and fear march together, the prisoner and the guard. Your line was chained together. Did you spot a fear walking beside a hope? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

Listen, for one day, to the way you talk to yourself. You idiot, you forgot again. Why are you like this. Look at you. Most of us would never speak to a friend that way. We'd lose the friend. But the voice in our own head gets away with it for years. In his sixth letter, Seneca passes along a line from the same Stoic as yesterday, Hecaton, and it's the answer Hecaton gave when someone asked him how far he'd come. Today: a friend to myself.
screen: `YOU IDIOT. WHY ARE YOU LIKE THIS.` → `WE'D NEVER SAY IT TO A FRIEND.` → `A FRIEND TO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the change. Letter six opens with Seneca saying he feels himself not just improving but being transformed. And he adds, honestly, that he still has much to correct. That, he says, is itself a sign of progress: you can finally see faults you couldn't see before. Second, the question. Then he shares what pleased him in Hecaton that day. Someone asks: what progress have you made? And Hecaton answers, in Gummere's translation: I have begun to be a friend to myself. Not I've mastered my passions. Not I've read everything. Just that. Third, why it's big. Seneca says this is great progress, because such a person will never be alone. And, he adds, you can be sure that someone who is a friend to himself is a friend to everyone. The friendship starts at home and spreads outward. Fourth, what kind of friend. This isn't flattery, or excusing everything. A few days ago Seneca told Lucilius to choose friends carefully and then trust them wholly. A good friend tells you the truth and stays on your side while doing it. That's the friend Hecaton means: honest about your faults, patient with them, and not cruel. Many traditions have their own words for this, for treating yourself with the care you'd give a neighbor. The Stoic version is simple: be to yourself what a true friend would be. Notice it says begun. Even Hecaton was only starting.
screen: `SEEING FAULTS IS PROGRESS.` · `WHAT PROGRESS HAVE YOU MADE?` · `NEVER ALONE; A FRIEND TO ALL.` · `HONEST, PATIENT, NOT CRUEL.` · then, large: `A FRIEND TO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been hard on yourself about lately. Hear the voice you've been using. Now imagine a good friend heard all of it. What would they say? Probably something honest, and something kind, both at once. Let that friend's voice speak to you now, quietly, about the same thing. Then decide on one kind thing you can do for yourself today: a glass of water, an early night, a walk, a real lunch. Breathe, and let yourself be on your own side. The bell holds the time.
A friend to myself. Hecaton's answer, passed on by Seneca: the sign of progress is to have begun treating yourself as a true friend would, honest and kind. Today's word.
Your line: a friend to myself. Do the one kind thing you chose. And the next time the harsh voice starts, answer it the way a good friend would. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Some who practice Stoicism measure progress not by perfection but by how they treat themselves: honest about faults, patient with them, and on their own side.

original.note: Latin: I have begun to be a friend to myself, Hecaton's words in Seneca's sixth letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: self-care, Roman edition.
what it means: Hecaton's measure of progress is treating yourself as a true friend would, honest about faults and kind about them.
what a scholar hears: the line survives only because Seneca quoted it; Hecaton's own books on duties and goods are lost.
